If you liked this "visualization of pi",  I also made an UHD 1440p widescreen version of this pi simulation which is 3 minutes longer. Here is the link , hope you'd engage there too and help that go viral as well !  :)  

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tuR5NI-bvu8

---------------------------------------------------

If you are looking for a short explanation of the Post :

The outer arm spins around at a speed, precisely π times faster than the inner arm. But because π is this never-ending, irrational number, that outer arm will never, ever stop at its starting point, no matter how long the video goes on. It's like a forever chase scene where the arm always misses the target line by the tiniest bit, and that bit is basically as thin as it gets.

The Detailed explanation of this Pi post by "angzt" from reddit :

https://www.reddit.com/r/oddlysatisfying/comments/17dif1m/comment/k5y7s8i/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=web2x&context=3

---------------------------------------------------

Python code for the final drawing made by this mechanism ( Not for the animation ) :

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Create an array of theta values in degrees (e.g., from 0 to 113*360 degrees)
theta_degrees = np.linspace(0, 113*360, 10000)

# Convert degrees to radians
theta_radians = np.deg2rad(theta_degrees)

# Calculate z(theta) using the formula , 1j is imaginary number
z = np.exp(theta_radians * 1j) + np.exp(np.pi * theta_radians * 1j)

# Separate the real and imaginary parts of z
x = np.real(z)
y = np.imag(z)

# Create a plot with specific settings
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 10))  # Set a square figure 10x10 inches
plt.plot(x, y, color='white', linewidth=0.5)  # Set line color to white and line width to 0.5

plt.gca().set_facecolor('black') # Set background color to black
plt.gca().set_aspect('equal')  # Equal aspect ratio
plt.grid(False)  # Turn off the grids

plt.ylim(-2.5, 2.5) # Y-axis limit

plt.show() # Display the plot

title: Why do Tightrope Walkers Hold Long Poles?
caption:
1
00:00:00,009 --> 00:00:04,538
Why is it that tightrope walkers are always carrying a long pole?

2
00:00:04,538 --> 00:00:10,281
Well, you fall when you're center of mass, your body's balance point, goes outside the base of

3
00:00:10,281 --> 00:00:11,701
support - or your feet.

4
00:00:11,702 --> 00:00:16,699
At that point, there's nothing to support you against the pull of gravity and you topple over.

5
00:00:16,699 --> 00:00:20,158
But if you add a pole with weights on each end, look what happens.

6
00:00:20,329 --> 00:00:24,609
Adding the weights pulls your cumulative center of mass below your support base.

7
00:00:24,620 --> 00:00:27,739
So toppling over now requires it to move up.

8
00:00:27,750 --> 00:00:29,370
Gravity is now your friend.

9
00:00:29,379 --> 00:00:33,442
It constantly pulls the center of mass back down to stabilize things out.

10
00:00:33,451 --> 00:00:36,993
It's the same thing with these balancing bird toys, the wings are weighted.

11
00:00:37,002 --> 00:00:41,262
So the center of mass is actually below its balancing point at the beak.

12
00:00:41,271 --> 00:00:45,923
Although holding the pole low does lower their center of mass, they don't use huge weights.

13
00:00:45,932 --> 00:00:49,278
And that's because the biggest benefit of the pole comes from the length.

14
00:00:49,279 --> 00:00:50,752
These two rods weigh the same.

15
00:00:50,762 --> 00:00:55,533
But when I spin it with the same force, the shorter one rotates way faster than the longer one.

16
00:00:55,542 --> 00:01:00,335
That's because the longer one has more rotational inertia, meaning it's harder to rotate.

17
00:01:00,345 --> 00:01:04,286
So if you hold a long pole, that actually makes you harder to rotate as well.

18
00:01:04,295 --> 00:01:08,756
And you actually know this, which is why when you're trying to balance, you automatically put

19
00:01:08,756 --> 00:01:09,435
your arms out.

20
00:01:09,444 --> 00:01:12,974
But there's another trick to say on a tight rope that doesn't require a pole at all.

21
00:01:12,986 --> 00:01:17,002
And it's actually one of the really fun CrunchLabs toys that gets delivered right to your porch where

22

you build it yourself as I teach you all the juicy physics that make them work.

23

For example, the secret to this tight rope walker.

00:00:00,659 --> 00:00:06,140
Okay so today, I'm gonna be doing something, that I think is kind of gross.

2

To get started the first thing that I'll need to do, is add some water to a beaker.

3

Now the next thing that I'll need, is a super stinky chemical, called hexamethylenediamine.

4
00:00:17,320 --> 00:00:23,187
I'll add about 4.4g of it to the water, and I'll stir it until it all disappears.

It's now all gone, and I'll move on to making the other solution that I need.

6

This one's also pretty simple, and the first ingredient, is something called cyclohexane.

7
00:00:41,390 --> 00:00:47,040
I'll add about 100mL of it, and then I'll pour in the last ingredient, called adipoyl

8
00:00:47,040 --> 00:00:48,489
chloride.

9
00:00:48,489 --> 00:00:53,699
I'll mix this up a bit, and now, I'm ready to do something nasty.

10
00:00:53,699 --> 00:00:58,520
To do this, I need to add 10mL of each solution, to a small beaker.

11
00:00:58,520 --> 00:01:03,840
I'll start with the stink water based one, and on top of it, I'll carefully pour in the

12

cyclohexane one.

13
00:01:05,690 --> 00:01:11,640
These two liquids aren't able to mix, and like water and oil, they stay separated.

14
00:01:11,640 --> 00:01:15,579
Now, all I need to do is use some tweezers.

15
00:01:20,540 --> 00:01:27,600
I'm able to pull out a gross slimy string, and if I wrap it on a glass rod, I can keep

16
00:01:27,600 --> 00:01:29,030
pulling it out.

17
00:01:29,030 --> 00:01:34,530
I really find that this looks pretty nasty, but it's actually just plastic.

18
00:01:34,530 --> 00:01:40,430
More specifically, it's nylon, and it's forming between the two liquids.

19
00:01:40,430 --> 00:01:45,720
I can keep pulling it, until the chemicals run out, and I'm left with something, that

20
00:01:45,720 --> 00:01:48,500
kind of looks like a cocoon.

21
00:01:48,500 --> 00:01:53,688
It's still full of water and cyclohexane though, and it's all soft and squishy.

22
00:01:57,597 --> 00:02:01,887
Now if I try pulling it apart, it's not actually very strong.

23
00:02:01,887 --> 00:02:06,500
This is because all the fibers, are extremely thin and fragile.

24
00:02:06,500 --> 00:02:11,841
If they were a lot thicker though, like they are in clothing, or in a fishing line, it

25
00:02:11,841 --> 00:02:13,851
would be a lot harder to do this.

There's a lot of different ways when it comes to math hacks. Here are just a few examples:

-If you're trying to do long division and are having trouble keeping track of all the digits, try using a pencil to keep track of your place. Draw a line under the number you're currently working on, and then draw a line above the number you're dividing by. This will help you keep your place and make sure you don't make any mistakes.

-If you're trying to add or subtract a large number of digits, try breaking the number down into smaller chunks. For example, if you're trying to add 753 + 872, you could break it down into 700 + 800 + 50 + 70 + 2. This will make it much easier to add up, and you're less likely to make a mistake.

-If you're having trouble memorizing your multiplication tables, try using a simple mnemonic device. For example, for the 7 times table, you could use the phrase "Seven times up, never down," which would remind you that 7 x 7 = 49. There are lots of different mnemonic devices out there, so find one that works for you.
